content.title: About
content.content: Egg roll with shrimp is a classic Asian snack made from a thin omelette wrapped around sautéed shrimp, vegetables, and sometimes noodles. The roll is served hot, crispy on the outside and tender inside, often accompanied by soy sauce or a sweet‑sour dipping sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The egg roll originated in Chinese street food in the early 20th century and quickly spread to Japan and the United States.
The delicate omelette wrapper cooks in just a few seconds on a very hot pan.
Shrimp are usually marinated in soy sauce, ginger, and garlic before being added to the roll, enhancing their flavor.
Traditional rolls often include crunchy vegetables such as carrots, cabbage, and bean sprouts for textural contrast.
In some regions the roll is finished with a fragrant oil, like sesame or garlic oil.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many fried snacks, an egg roll contains moderate fat, especially when cooked with minimal oil.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Shrimp contain omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The roll supplies B12 and B6 vitamins, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Shrimp are rich in selenium, zinc, and iron, which aid immune function and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp are a common allergen; individuals with shellfish allergy should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces and marinades can increase sodium levels, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking of shrimp can lead to foodborne illness.

items.title: High calories when deep‑fried
items.content: If the roll is deep‑fried, its calorie count rises significantly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the roll hot, sliced into bite‑size pieces. Dip it in soy sauce, sweet‑sour sauce, or chili sauce. For a lighter version, steam the roll first and then briefly pan‑fry to achieve a golden crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Freshly prepared rolls are best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat gently in an oven or skillet to restore crispness before serving.
